name: Dâw
confidence_why: The reference grammar (S. Martins 2004) and an independent instrumental study (Simmons & Epps 2025) both put stress on the final syllable of every polysyllabic word, and the only dissent, V. Martins's 1994 MA thesis, calls that same word-final high pitch a pitch accent rather than stress, so the placement is uncontested and only its label is.

new_statements.quote: Where lexemes have more than one syllable, primary stress falls on the final syllable. [ms p. 3] ... Stress in Dâw is consistently word-final. Unstressed syllables bear a default low tone, as in the first syllable of /tʃokwét/ [tʃ'òkˈwét] 'toucan'. Word-final syllables lacking a consonantal coda consistently have falling tone (and a long vowel), as in /tûː/ 'ground'. Note that words in Dâw have exactly one H pitch, always occurring on the stressed syllable. We analyze this as a constraint that a lexeme have one obligatory and cumulative H tone that must dock onto the stressed syllable. Any tone-bearing unit not linked to this H tone receives a L tone by default. [ms p. 5-6]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed final). Refines it with the tonal side: one obligatory, cumulative H docked on the stressed final syllable; length and tone contrasts restricted to that syllable; the system is described as a 'word-accent' system parasitic on lexical stress. The authors also note (ms p. 5-6) that their stress-based analysis differs from that of S. Martins (2004) and V. Martins (2005), who treat the contours as underlying tone with H as a phonetic effect of stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is always on the final syllable of the word (family-wide: primary stress on the final syllable of any polysyllabic lexeme). Dâw is at the same time a 'word-accent' tone language: every word carries exactly one H pitch, which sits on the stressed (final) syllable; unstressed syllables get default L. Tone (H on short vowels; rising vs falling on long vowels) and vowel length contrast only in that stressed syllable. Ms p. 4: 'only one long vowel and/or contrastive tone is realized per morpheme (and, in most cases, also per phonological word), and always coincides with stress.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Dâw (secondary stress is mentioned only for Swedish/Norwegian in the typological discussion, ms p. 4).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Dâw. For the sister languages the authors specify 'stem-final (word-final when no bound morphology is present)' (ms p. 7, on Hup and Yuhup, introduced with 'As in Dâw'), which suggests the stress domain is the stem when bound morphology is present. Word-final open syllables always have falling tone and a long vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: Neither opened work distinguishes Dâw varieties; both describe the language as a whole (Martins 1994 from his own fieldwork data, Simmons & Epps 2025 from S. Martins 2004 / V. Martins 2005 and their own data). Simmons & Epps's family-level statement (final stress in all four Naduhup languages) is also explicitly applied to Dâw.

new_statements.quote: No cruzamento dos dados apresentados, com a classificação tipológica, Dâw é uma língua pitch-accent (tonal periférica) e não é do tipo tonal verdadeiro, pelo fato de restringir o uso do tom: [...] 2. Palavras dissilábicas do tipo CV(C).CVC têm tom alto na última sílaba [á] e baixo na primeira [à] (cf. 4.3.1.). [p. 123] ... Dâw é uma língua pitch-accent, isto quer dizer que o acento em Dâw se faz pelo pitch. [p. 125] ... Deduz-se desta regra que o tom alto funciona como o acento. 5.3.1 Acento-entonação. O acento que é conhecido como "stress", e/ou loudness, é produzido pelo impulso pulmonar e manifesta-se em Dâw no nível da oração. [...] em Dâw o pitch funciona no nível da palavra e o stress no nível da oração. [p. 126]
new_statements.translation: Crossing the data presented with the typological classification, Dâw is a pitch-accent (peripheral tonal) language and not a true tone language, because it restricts the use of tone: [...] 2. Disyllabic words of the type CV(C).CVC have high tone on the last syllable [á] and low on the first [à] (cf. 4.3.1). [p. 123] ... Dâw is a pitch-accent language, which means that the accent in Dâw is realised by pitch. [p. 125] ... It follows from this rule that the high tone functions as the accent. 5.3.1 Accent-intonation. The accent known as 'stress' and/or loudness is produced by the pulmonary impulse and in Dâw manifests itself at the level of the clause. [...] in Dâw pitch operates at the word level and stress at the clause level. [p. 126]

new_statements.relation_note: Type, not placement, differs. The catalog records fixed final word STRESS; Martins denies word-level stress altogether (stress/loudness is a clause-level intonational phenomenon) and instead posits word-level pitch accent, one H per word. His placement of that H (last syllable in disyllables, p. 123; H on monosyllables) is compatible with the catalog's final position, so the disagreement is about the category (pitch accent vs stress-accent), which Simmons & Epps 2025 explicitly reject in favour of stress with a parasitic H.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Martins analyses Dâw as a pitch accent language: the word carries one high tone, which in CVC monosyllables is level H and in CV(C).CVC disyllables falls on the last syllable (L on the first); the high tone 'functions as the accent'. Intensity stress (loudness) is not a word-level property for him: it operates only at clause level, rising from the first to the last word of an independent clause and falling across a dependent clause (§5.3.2-5.3.3, pp. 133-135; conclusion p. 138: 'O acento (intensidade).. funciona no nível da oração'). He also claims pitch and stress are independent of each other (p. 132).
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal, not stress-related: CV: monosyllables have contour tones; CVVC words with voiceless coda always have low-high (rising) tone, with voiced coda high-low in 70% and low-high in 30% of cases (pp. 123-124, 138); a high-tone noun suffix is said to be dismantling the coda-conditioned system (p. 138-139).
new_statements.identity_note: Neither opened work distinguishes Dâw varieties; both describe the language as a whole (Martins 1994 from his own fieldwork data, Simmons & Epps 2025 from S. Martins 2004 / V. Martins 2005 and their own data). Simmons & Epps's family-level statement (final stress in all four Naduhup languages) is also explicitly applied to Dâw.

new_statements.quote: (18) [waˈʃap] – ‘cashew’ (19) [baˈpolˀ] – ‘steam boat’ [MARTINS, 2004, p. 74] ... Dâw has phonemic tone, which falls on primary stressed syllables and can be either falling or rising (see MARTINS, 2004). As shown earlier in this section, tone interacts with vowel length, i.e., falling and rising occur with long vowels, whereas short vowels are atonal (MARTINS, 2004, p. 79). In cases with phonological words composed of two tonal roots, tone occurs only on the last root and coincides with the accented syllable, creating a system of pitch accent (see MARTINS, 2014, p. 13; ANDRADE, 2014, p. 9).

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog records fixed: final syllable stress (final stress). Obert's overview is compatible: the accent falls on the last root of a complex phonological word and the disyllabic examples are finally stressed. It adds that the stressed syllable is the locus of a lexical rising/falling tone contrast tied to vowel length (short vowels atonal) and characterizes the system as pitch accent; it also flags a dispute in the literature over whether tone is lexical (Martins 2004) or sentence-level predictable (Costa 2014; Storto et al. 2013). This is a secondary summary in a dissertation on spatial language, not an original prosodic analysis.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Obert (summarizing Martins 2004, Andrade 2014) treats Dâw as having a primary-stressed (accented) syllable that is the sole host of a phonemic contour-tone contrast (rising vs falling, realized on allophonically long vowels; short vowels are atonal). In phonological words built from two tonal roots only the last root carries tone, and that coincides with the accented syllable, i.e. the accent sits at the right edge of the word; the two disyllabic transcriptions given ([waˈʃap], [baˈpolˀ]) both show final stress. The author labels the result a pitch accent system. No explicit general statement of the form 'stress falls on the final syllable' is made; roots are overwhelmingly monosyllabic CVC.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (only 'primary stressed syllables' is mentioned; no secondary stress rule given).
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. Notes that loanwords need not have identical vowels across syllables (still transcribed with final stress, e.g. [baˈpolˀ]); mentions that Costa (2014) and Storto et al. (2013) argue tone is predictable at sentence level, contradicting Martins' lexical-tone analysis (p. 58, section on valency), and that emphatic discourse carries sentential stress with vowel lengthening and laryngealization (p. 72).
new_statements.identity_note: Obert's data come from fieldwork in the single Dâw community of Waruá (São Gabriel da Cachoeira, upper Rio Negro, Amazonas, Brazil); the phonology overview is explicitly adapted from Martins (2004) and Andrade (2014) on the same variety. No dialect split is described.

tone_statements.citation: Nikulin, Andrey. 2026. A phonological reconstruction of Proto-Dâw–Hup / Фонологическая реконструкция праязыка дыу–хупской группы. Journal of Language Relationship 23(3-4): 307-343.
tone_statements.quote: Dâw, Yuhup, and Hup are tonal languages. In Dâw, only long vowels carry tone (either rising or falling), whereas short vowels are toneless; in fact, Martins (2004: 55–56) posits a triple opposition between toneless, rising-toned and falling-toned syllables, where vowel length is considered allophonic. … However, there are words with voiced codas and rising tone in Dâw. In this paper, I follow Martins (2004: 78–79) in positing a tonal distinction for Dâw and, consequently, for PDH, however low its functional load may turn out to be.
tone_statements.locator: p. 334, sec. 5 'Tones and vowel length', first two paragraphs
tone_statements.summary: Dâw taken as tonal after Martins 2004: long vowels bear rising or falling tone, short vowels toneless; all three contrast only before voiced codas; contrast called suspect; rising tone derives nouns.

tone_statements.citation: Barboza, Lucas Cavalini. 2017. Aspectos da glotalização na língua Dâw: um estudo de fonética experimental [Aspects of glottalization in Dâw: an experimental phonetics study]. Dissertação de Mestrado (MA), Faculdade de Filosofia, Letras e Ciências Humanas, Universidade de São Paulo. Orientadora: Luciana Raccanello Storto. Defended 2017-05-12.
tone_statements.quote: A língua Dâw possui um sistema tonal restrito com possibilidades de distinção lexical e funcional. Segundo Martins (2004, p. 78-79), as palavras classificam-se como tonais ou atonais, admitindo as primeiras os tons de contorno ascendente e descendente. Desta maneira, há um sistema de distinção baseado em três paradigmas. … Na língua Dâw, somente as sílabas finais das palavras monomorfêmicas apresentam tom fonêmico. … A existência de pares mínimos e análogos e a consistência dos tons em diferentes contextos reforçam o argumento de Martins (2004) de que existe um sistema tonal na língua Dâw.
tone_statements.translation: Dâw has a restricted tonal system with possibilities of lexical and functional distinction. According to Martins (2004: 78-79), words are classed as tonal or atonal, the former admitting the rising and falling contour tones. Thus there is a system of distinction based on three paradigms. … In Dâw only the final syllables of monomorphemic words carry phonemic tone. … The existence of minimal and analogous pairs and the consistency of the tones across contexts reinforce Martins's (2004) argument that a tonal system exists in Dâw.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 81 and 83, sec. 6.1 'O sistema tonal e acentual da língua Dâw' (Table 10 minimal pairs p. 81)
tone_statements.summary: Restricted tone system: words are atonal or bear a rising or falling contour tone, contrastive only on the final syllable; F0 tracks and minimal pairs confirm it; separate final-syllable stress.

tone_statements.citation: Martins, Silvana Andrade & Valteir Martins. 2015. Tons e empréstimos em dâw: um estudo para o (re)conhecimento das línguas indígenas do Amazonas. Manaus: UEA – Universidade do Estado do Amazonas. 134 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Os morfemas possuem tom zero (atonais), tom de contorno ascendente /VI e tom de contorno descendente /~ /. As realizac;oes dos tons de contorno tern como implementac;ao fonetica o alongamento das vogais que os portam. As palavras, em sua maioria, sao monossilabicas e possuem somente um tom … Tambem, na palavra, a posic;ao do tom e parcialmente controlada pelo sistema de stress. … o sistema tonal de Daw caracteriza-se por contrastar um tom zero e dois tons de contorno, ao inves de tons de niveis; por especificar os tons de todos os itens lexicais e funcionais na entrada lexical
tone_statements.translation: Morphemes have zero tone (toneless), rising contour tone and falling contour tone. The contour tones are phonetically implemented by lengthening of the vowels that bear them. Words are mostly monosyllabic and have only one tone ... Also, within the word, the position of the tone is partly controlled by the stress system. ... the Daw tone system is characterised by contrasting a zero tone and two contour tones, rather than level tones; by specifying the tones of all lexical and functional items in the lexical entry
tone_statements.locator: p.16 (Parte 1, Introducao) left half, and p.58 (5 Consideracoes Finais) left half
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone: two contour tones, rising and falling, vs toneless (tom zero) morphemes; contours are units, realised with vowel lengthening; one tone per morpheme; tonal suprafixes; fixed final stress.

tone_statements.citation: Martins, Valteir. 2005. Reconstrução Fonológica do Protomaku Oriental. PhD dissertation, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Utrecht: LOT (LOT Dissertation Series 104). xvii+385 pp. ISBN 978-90-76864-71-6; OCLC 62587989.
tone_statements.quote: Em Dâw, há somente dois tons lexicalmente especificados: ascendente / / e descendente / /. As palavras que não têm esses tipos de tons são consideradas atonais, pois os outros tons (alto [´] e baixo [`]) são resultados do sistema acentual, uma vez que a sílaba não-acentuada sempre possui tom baixo e a acentuada, tom alto (cf. Seção 2.1.4). … Portanto, as ocorrências dos tons ascendentes e descendentes evidenciam que eles são fonológicos, enquanto que os tons alto e baixo são fonéticos.
tone_statements.translation: In Dâw there are only two lexically specified tones: rising and falling. Words that lack these tones are considered toneless, since the other tones (high and low) result from the stress system, given that the unstressed syllable always has low tone and the stressed one high tone (cf. 2.1.4). … Thus the occurrences of the rising and falling tones show that they are phonological, whereas the high and low tones are phonetic.
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical tones, rising and falling, beside fixed final stress; high and low pitch follow from stress; tones also mark deverbals and transitivity; rising vs falling contrast only with voiced codas.

readall_conflicts: One analytical disagreement, not a placement disagreement. Martins (1994, pp. 123-126, 132-133, 138) treats Dâw as a pitch accent language whose one H tone per word 'functions as the accent' and says intensity stress exists only at clause level (pitch = word level, stress = clause level, the reverse of Portuguese). Simmons & Epps (2025, ms pp. 3-6) treat the same facts as fixed word-final lexical stress with an obligatory cumulative H that docks on the stressed syllable ('a word-accent system parasitic on lexical stress'), and state outright that 'Stress in Dâw is consistently word-final'; they note (ms p. 5-6) that their analysis differs from S. Martins 2004 / V. Martins 2005 in exactly this respect. Both sources put the word-level prominence (H tone) on the final syllable of polysyllables, so the catalog's final placement is supported by both; only the label (stress vs pitch accent) is contested. Obert 2019 could not be opened.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed final stress on the prosodic word, non-distinctive/demarcative, no weight, a closed listed set of extrametric suffixes, tone lexical and co-occurring with stress in simple/compound words) is taken verbatim from the dedicated stress section of the only reference grammar of Dâw (Martins 2004, LOT 98, 685 pp), which we hold as an open full-text PDF; the quotation and page/PDF locators check out exactly, and the morphology chapter of the same work restates the extrametric-suffix rule consistently. Glottolog lists no later grammar or phonology; the web check (cut short by the session) found only comparative tone work and Obert's 2019 space dissertation, both of which cite Martins 2004 for Dâw. Obert 2019 is open but its host was unreachable today; it is the one item worth downloading later for independent confirmation. no reclassification or identity issue.

sources.quote: Dâw, Yuhup, and Hup are tonal languages. In Dâw, only long vowels carry tone (either rising or falling), whereas short vowels are toneless; in fact, Martins (2004: 55–56) posits a triple opposition between toneless, rising-toned and falling-toned syllables, where vowel length is considered allophonic. … However, there are words with voiced codas and rising tone in Dâw. In this paper, I follow Martins (2004: 78–79) in positing a tonal distinction for Dâw and, consequently, for PDH, however low its functional load may turn out to be.

sources.note: Dâw taken as tonal after Martins 2004: long vowels bear rising or falling tone, short vowels toneless; all three contrast only before voiced codas; contrast called suspect; rising tone derives nouns.

sources.quote: A língua Dâw possui um sistema tonal restrito com possibilidades de distinção lexical e funcional. Segundo Martins (2004, p. 78-79), as palavras classificam-se como tonais ou atonais, admitindo as primeiras os tons de contorno ascendente e descendente. Desta maneira, há um sistema de distinção baseado em três paradigmas. … Na língua Dâw, somente as sílabas finais das palavras monomorfêmicas apresentam tom fonêmico. … A existência de pares mínimos e análogos e a consistência dos tons em diferentes contextos reforçam o argumento de Martins (2004) de que existe um sistema tonal na língua Dâw.

tone.translation: Dâw has a restricted tonal system with possibilities of lexical and functional distinction. According to Martins (2004: 78-79), words are classed as tonal or atonal, the former admitting the rising and falling contour tones. Thus there is a system of distinction based on three paradigms. … In Dâw only the final syllables of monomorphemic words carry phonemic tone. … The existence of minimal and analogous pairs and the consistency of the tones across contexts reinforce Martins's (2004) argument that a tonal system exists in Dâw.

tone.translation: Morphemes have zero tone (toneless), rising contour tone and falling contour tone. The contour tones are phonetically implemented by lengthening of the vowels that bear them. Words are mostly monosyllabic and have only one tone ... Also, within the word, the position of the tone is partly controlled by the stress system. ... the Daw tone system is characterised by contrasting a zero tone and two contour tones, rather than level tones; by specifying the tones of all lexical and functional items in the lexical entry
tone.summary: Lexical tone: two contour tones, rising and falling, vs toneless (tom zero) morphemes; contours are units, realised with vowel lengthening; one tone per morpheme; tonal suprafixes; fixed final stress.

sources.quote: Em Dâw, há somente dois tons lexicalmente especificados: ascendente / / e descendente / /. As palavras que não têm esses tipos de tons são consideradas atonais, pois os outros tons (alto [´] e baixo [`]) são resultados do sistema acentual, uma vez que a sílaba não-acentuada sempre possui tom baixo e a acentuada, tom alto (cf. Seção 2.1.4). … Portanto, as ocorrências dos tons ascendentes e descendentes evidenciam que eles são fonológicos, enquanto que os tons alto e baixo são fonéticos.
sources.note: Two lexical tones, rising and falling, beside fixed final stress; high and low pitch follow from stress; tones also mark deverbals and transitivity; rising vs falling contrast only with voiced codas.

tone.translation: In Dâw there are only two lexically specified tones: rising and falling. Words that lack these tones are considered toneless, since the other tones (high and low) result from the stress system, given that the unstressed syllable always has low tone and the stressed one high tone (cf. 2.1.4). … Thus the occurrences of the rising and falling tones show that they are phonological, whereas the high and low tones are phonetic.
